summary: Describes an architecture and framework for letting applications talk to middleboxes such as firewalls and address translators. Such devices cannot always handle protocols like SIP or H.323 by looking at packet headers alone, so the framework lets trusted agents help them make decisions.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine a guard at a gate who cannot tell which visitors are expected. This document describes a way for a helper to tell the guard who is allowed in, so the right visitors get through.

questions: how can applications talk to firewalls
what is a middlebox policy decision point
subtitle: A framework for letting trusted helper agents tell firewalls and NATs which dynamic traffic to allow.

tldr.problem: Firewalls and NATs cannot recognise applications such as SIP and H.323 by looking at packet headers alone, so vendors build application knowledge into the middlebox, which is hard to maintain and error prone.
tldr.mechanism: The framework moves that knowledge into external MIDCOM agents. An agent uses a MIDCOM protocol to ask the middlebox to open pinholes or create NAT bindings, while a policy decision point says which agents are authorised.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3303 only defines the architecture. It states that the MIDCOM protocol is yet to be devised, and a companion document lists the protocol requirements.

today: RFC 3303 is an Informational document and the data does not list it as obsoleted or updated. It defines a framework and leaves the protocol undefined; the protocol requirements are in RFC 3304.

sections.title: Why Middleboxes Need Help
sections.content:
A middlebox is an intermediate network device that performs services such as packet filtering (a firewall) or network address translation (NAT). Real-time applications such as SIP and H.323, and peer-to-peer applications such as Napster and NetMeeting, cannot be identified by merely examining packet headers. So middleboxes typically embed application intelligence inside the device.

The RFC argues that this tight coupling makes middleboxes hard to maintain. New applications need operating system updates, operators depend on the middlebox vendor, and packing many application protocols into one box adds complexity that is likely to be error prone and to degrade performance.

The goal is an application-independent protocol so that middleboxes can stay focused on firewall and NAT services while external agents carry the application knowledge. The discussion is limited to firewall and NAT services, but the framework is meant to be extensible to other services.
sections.plainLanguage: A gate guard who has to learn the rules of every game that visitors play gets overwhelmed. It is easier to let helpers who know each game tell the guard what to do.

sections.title: The Cast of Characters
sections.content:
A MIDCOM agent is an entity that performs application level gateway (ALG) functions while being logically external to the middlebox. An ALG is not visible to end-hosts and does not terminate sessions, which sets it apart from a proxy. The RFC considers only In-Path agents, meaning agents on a node that the relevant packets flow through. Application proxies, gateways and even end-hosts can host an agent, and SIP proxies and H.323 gatekeepers are named as good candidates because they already understand the application.

The MIDCOM PDP (Policy Decision Point) is a logical entity that holds policy profiles and advises the middlebox on authorising or ending an agent's access. It does not help the middlebox implement its services, and the protocol between the middlebox and the PDP is unrelated to the MIDCOM protocol.

Policy rules combine filters (packet matching information such as a 5-tuple) with actions (such as a firewall permit or deny, or a NAT address bind). They are communicated through the MIDCOM protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The helper is the agent, the boss who says which helpers can be trusted is the policy server, and the guard is the middlebox.

sections.title: The MIDCOM Architecture
sections.content:
A middlebox may run several functions, such as firewall, NAT, VPN tunneling and intrusion detection, on several interfaces. Agents reach them through one MIDCOM protocol interface, and a separate policy interface connects to the PDP. A single agent session should be usable to reach different services on the same middlebox.

The MIDCOM protocol is client-server and initiated by the agent. It has a session setup phase, a run-time phase and a termination phase. Either side may end a session, and a session also ends if a party goes out of service or the PDP says the agent is no longer authorised. A MIDCOM session is a lasting association and is not assumed to be a TCP connection.

Before any session, the agent must be registered with the middlebox or the PDP. Registration is often a manual operator task and records the agent's authorisation policy, hosting entity, accessibility profile and security profile. The agent should open its session before the application starts, or it may be unable to process the control stream in time. The RFC states that the MIDCOM protocol is a protocol yet to be devised.
sections.plainLanguage: A helper has to be signed up with the boss first. Then it can walk up to the guard, start a conversation, ask for things during the visit and say goodbye at the end.

sections.title: A SIP Call Through a Middlebox
sections.content:
Section 7 walks through an external caller reaching a SIP phone in a private domain. The SIP proxy hosts the MIDCOM agent. The agent parses the SDP part of the SIP messages to learn the dynamic UDP ports for the RTP and RTCP media streams, then uses the MIDCOM protocol to act.

  • With a firewall, the agent asks to permit the media flows (opening pinholes). It asks before the INVITE reaches the callee, because early media sent before the 200 OK would otherwise be blocked.
  • With NAPT, the agent queries the port binding for the SIP address on port 5060, creates NAT session descriptors for the media flows, and rewrites the SDP in the 200 OK with the NAPT port binding. When the call ends it terminates the SIP session bundle, and the middlebox is assumed to delete the associated media sessions.
  • With both, NAT operations come before firewall operations, because the firewall rules are written for packet fields as seen on the wire at the external interface.
sections.plainLanguage: The helper reads the phone call's invitation to find out which doors the call will use. Then it asks the guard to open exactly those doors, and to close them again when the call is over.

sections.title: Operational Considerations and Scope
sections.content:
The RFC lists several practical points. The middlebox may send asynchronous notifications to agents about events such as session creation or termination and failures. A middlebox should use timers on dynamically allocated resources so it can recover them if the agent that requested them is no longer alive. For a middlebox that runs both services, NAT precedes the firewall on egress and follows it on ingress.

The framework addresses applications with separate signaling and data sessions, such as SIP, and applications that signal in-band, such as H.323 with H.245. An agent is not required to intervene in data traffic.

The applicability statement limits the framework to a single middlebox, running NAT or firewall, along the application route, in a DMZ at the edge of a private domain. Other topologies need case-by-case review. Discovery of middleboxes and agents, and communication among middleboxes, are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The guard should tidy up doors that a helper opened if the helper disappears. This plan is meant for one guard standing at the edge of one neighbourhood.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Without MIDCOM, a middlebox needs data in the clear to inspect or modify it. The framework removes the need for the middlebox to inspect or rewrite transport payload, which lets applications protect themselves end-to-end with the help of a trusted agent, especially one on the end-host. It does not fix NAT breaking IPsec, because the middlebox still changes IP and transport headers.

Between agent and middlebox the RFC discusses authorisation, authentication, integrity and confidentiality. Without authentication an attacker could spoof an agent and open holes in the firewall or fill a NAT table, or pose as a middlebox and divert data. Without replay protection an attacker could reopen or close a pinhole at will. Candidate mechanisms are IPsec AH and ESP, TLS and application-layer security, and message security shall use existing standards where they meet the requirements.

Conflicting directives from multiple agents on the same application session are another risk, which is reduced when a single agent handles all middlebox services for an application.
sections.plainLanguage: The guard must check that a helper really is the helper before opening doors. Otherwise a stranger could pretend to be the helper and let in trouble.
